Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette: Rohan's life was forever changed when he was diagnosed with leukemia two years ago. He remembered the hospital room where the doctor delivered the news, the fluorescent lights overhead, and the antiseptic smell that filled his nostrils. What struck him most was the feeling of his body betraying him, as if he had been living in a fragile shell all along. The grueling months of chemotherapy that followed only reinforced this notion - every session felt like a battle to reclaim control over his own flesh. As Rohan slowly began to recover, he found himself increasingly avoiding anything that reminded him of those harrowing days. Hospitals, ambulances, and even physical examinations became triggers that sent his mind racing back to the darkest moments of his illness. He would steer clear of conversations about health, medical dramas on TV, or even news articles about illnesses. His friends and family grew concerned about his newfound aversion to discussing his experience, but Rohan couldn't shake off the feeling that revisiting those memories would somehow jinx his fragile recovery. At work, as a UX designer, Rohan's creativity began to suffer. He found himself constantly on edge, his body tense and ready to react to any perceived danger. Even minor setbacks in projects or delays in meeting deadlines made him assume the worst - that something was terribly wrong, just like it had been during his illness. His colleagues noticed a change in his demeanor, how he would bristle at suggestions or get defensive over feedback. Rohan knew this wasn't the person he used to be, but he couldn't seem to shake off the feeling of being on high alert all the time. Rohan's wife, Nalini, tried her best to reassure him that he was safe now, that the cancer was in remission, and that they would face any future challenges together. But Rohan just couldn't bring himself to believe it. There was a nagging voice inside his head, whispering that something was fundamentally wrong with him as a person, that he was weak and defective. This self-doubt seeped into other areas of his life - he felt emotionally numb, disconnected from the things that used to give him joy. As time went on, Rohan's avoidance behaviors took a toll on his relationships. Nalini grew frustrated with his reluctance to discuss important health matters or make plans for their future together. His friends and family felt shut out by his unwillingness to engage in conversations about his experience. Even simple activities like going for a walk or trying new restaurants became sources of stress, as Rohan worried about putting his body under undue strain. One day, when Nalini confronted him about the growing distance between them, Rohan realized he couldn't keep living like this. The numbness and tension had become unbearable. He knew it was time to seek help, not just for himself but also for those who cared about him. As he sat in his therapist's office, filling out forms and answering questions, Rohan felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to reclaim control over his life and find a way to trust himself again. But as he left the office that day, Rohan couldn't shake off the familiar feeling of dread - what if seeking help was just another sign of weakness? What if he wasn't strong enough to overcome this? The fear swirled inside him like a living thing, a constant reminder of the long and difficult journey ahead.
